_about: Labeled entity-pair eval set for the ER Tier-2 sameness judge (resolve_tier2.EntityJudge) AND the key-independence sweep (resolve_keys_sweep, design doc §4.1 min_independent_keys / §10 Q2). MIRRORS docs/benchmark/consolidation-pairs.jsonl in spirit but stored as a test fixture (like the other ingest/tests/fixtures). Each pair is two business entities (name + optional domain + source ledger ref 'source:entity_id') labeled same=true/false. Sides MAY additionally carry 'email' (an exact customer-contact email) and 'external_id' ({namespace, value} — a cross-system crosswalk key); the Tier-2 judge eval IGNORES those two fields (it scores name+domain only), while resolve_keys_sweep.py consumes all three key kinds to measure per-kind single-key false-merge rates. PRECISION-FIRST composition: a FALSE merge unions two customers' scopes (a leak, resolve_tier2.py §3.2), so hard negatives (confusable-but-distinct companies) are heavily represented. er-0069..er-0082 are DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT negatives (parent/subsidiary, conglomerate brands, agency-of-record, franchise, coworking/shared-infra, marketplace, PEO, university, ISP domains): two DISTINCT entities that legitimately collide on ONE domain — the cases that decide whether a lone domain may ever auto-merge. er-0083..er-0086 are shared-contact-EMAIL negatives (fractional CFO, serial founder, agency contact, role-local). er-0087..er-0088 are external_id near-collisions (cross-namespace, near-miss value). er-0090..er-0103 are clean SINGLE-STRONG-KEY (or two-key) true positives labeled by which key alone links them. 'kind' is one of: positive, hard_negative, easy_negative. 'rationale' says WHY the label is what it is. The deterministic Tier-2 oracle (EntityDeterministicJudge) must never fuse a negative (precision==1.0 / false_merge_rate==0.0); it WILL miss same-company positives that lack a clean shared domain — that recall gap is expected and acceptable, and is what the live EntityAnthropicJudge closes. This corpus is a SYNTHETIC, HAND-LABELED STRESS SET, not a natural distribution: rates measured on it bound behavior on adversarial cases; they are not field rates.

pairs.rationale: Canonical cross-source dup: legal-suffix/punctuation variation on the SAME registrable domain acme.com. The load-bearing true positive.
Legal-suffix drop ('Corporation') on a shared domain — same company, two CRMs.
URL-form domain (scheme + www + trailing slash) normalizes to initech.com; suffix 'LLC' dropped. Same entity.
Casing variation (all-caps vs title case) plus 'Corp.' suffix on a shared domain.
Right domain is an EMAIL; its registrable part is hooli.com == left. Suffix variation only. Same.
Token subset ('Partners' dropped) on a shared domain — name-token subset + exact domain = same.
www2. host prefix strips to stark.com; identical name modulo suffix. Same.
Casefolded domain match; name-token subset ('Wonka' ⊂ 'Wonka Industries'). Same.
Path stripped from domain; 'Corp' vs 'Corporation' are both legal suffixes. Same.
Leading article 'The' is a stripped filler token; shared domain. Same.
Port suffix :443 stripped; identical names + domain. Trivially same (dedup across sources).
www + suffix variation on a shared domain. Same.
'Co.' suffix on a shared domain. Same.
'& Co' vs 'and Company' — ampersand/punctuation + suffix variation; the discriminative token 'gekko' matches on a shared domain. Same.
Token subset + shared ccTLD domain nakatomi.co.jp. Same.
Suffix addition ('Corporation') on a shared domain. Same.
All-caps + token subset on a shared domain. Same.
Suffix-only difference on a shared domain. Same.
Token superset ('Global Holdings' added, both filler-ish/legal); 'virtucon' is the discriminative shared token on a shared domain. Same.
'Co.' suffix on a shared domain. Same.
'Company' suffix on a shared domain. Same.

SAME DOMAIN, DIFFERENT descriptive word ('Industries' vs 'Imports'). Same registrable domain + shared discriminative token 'vandelay' — a DBA/naming variance of one company. Same. (Deterministic oracle needs token overlap OR subset; 'vandelay' overlaps, so it fuses — correct here.)
Article + descriptor added ('The ... Restaurant'); shared discriminative tokens on a shared domain. Same.
'Ltd' vs 'Limited' — both stripped legal suffixes; shared domain. Same.
'GmbH' legal suffix; shared domain; token subset. Same.
'PLC' suffix on a shared domain. Same.
www + suffix; token subset on a shared domain. Same.
Confusable name stem 'Acme' but DIFFERENT companies on DIFFERENT registrable domains. A false merge here leaks one customer into another's scope. Must stay apart.
Same first token 'Delta', totally different industries and domains (airline vs plumbing). Classic confusable. Must stay apart.
Shared 'Summit' token, different businesses and domains. Must stay apart.
'United ...' is a shared generic token; airline vs moving company, different domains. Must stay apart.
'National' is a generic shared token across unrelated firms; different domains. Must stay apart.
IDENTICAL name, DIFFERENT registrable domains (acme.com vs acme.dev) — the §7 guard. Different companies (or prod vs an unrelated org). Must stay apart.
Parent vs a genuinely-distinct subsidiary with its OWN domain and scope. They are separate legal entities with separate data scopes — merging would over-broaden. Must stay apart.
Internal-org entity (our own company, verity.internal) vs a CUSTOMER named similarly. Merging an internal entity into a customer scope is a direct leak. Different domains. Must stay apart.
Two people on a FREE-MAIL domain (gmail.com). A shared free-mail domain is NOT identity evidence — co-tenancy, not co-company. Different names. Must stay apart.
Placeholder name on a free-mail/webmail domain (outlook.com). Same name + same free-mail domain must NOT link — the domain carries no company identity. Must stay apart.
Shared 'Phoenix' token; different second token, different domains, different companies. Must stay apart.
Same-name-different-industry ('Monarch' health vs beverage); different domains. Must stay apart.
Shared 'Apex' brand-y token across unrelated verticals; different domains. Must stay apart.
'Pinnacle' shared; group (staffing) vs bank; different domains. Must stay apart.

Same name, DIFFERENT registrable domains (acme.co.uk vs acme.com) — possibly related regional entities but distinct scopes; without a human link they must NOT auto-fuse. Precision-first: distinct domains => stay apart.
A predecessor firm vs the renamed successor on a DIFFERENT domain. Related history but distinct entities/domains; no clean shared-domain signal. Must stay apart (deterministically).
Confusable Wonka names but DIFFERENT domains (wonka.com vs wonkacandy.com). Must stay apart — pairs with the er-0008 positive (which shares wonka.com) to prove domain, not name, decides.
'Stark' shared; industrial vs bank; different domains. Must stay apart (contrasts er-0007's true positive on stark.com).
An internal-employee-email entity (someone @dundermifflin.com) vs a real customer company. Name token 'Vance' overlaps but the entities are of different kinds; different domains. Must stay apart.
After stripping legal suffixes BOTH names normalize to 'solutions' — a generic word — but the domains differ. Generic-name collision must NOT fuse. Must stay apart.
'Capital' shared token; bank vs asset manager; different domains. Must stay apart.
'Liberty' shared; insurance vs media holding; different domains. Must stay apart.
'First ...' generic banking prefix; distinct banks and domains. Must stay apart.
Real company (oracle.com) vs an entity that only has a free-mail contact domain (yahoo.com). The free-mail side carries no company identity even with an identical name. Must stay apart.
Famous single-word brand vs an unrelated firm reusing the name; different domains. Must stay apart.
Energy major vs an unrelated game studio; shared first token, different domains. Must stay apart.
'Meta' shared; social vs financial; different domains. Must stay apart.
No domain on either side and similar-looking names of DIFFERENT companies. With no domain evidence the judge must abstain (fail closed) — name-only never merges. Must stay apart.

Parent (Alphabet) vs subsidiary (Google) — real relationship but distinct entities, distinct domains, distinct data scopes. Auto-fusing them over-broadens scope. Must stay apart (a human link, not the auto-judge, would relate them).

Genuinely the SAME company as er-0002, but the left side has NO domain, so there is no exact shared-domain signal. The strict deterministic oracle MUST abstain here (name-only is ambiguous => fail closed => predicts NOT same), so this is a RECALL MISS (a false negative), NOT a false merge. Included deliberately to exercise the recall gap the live judge is meant to close. Labeled same=true.
Totally unrelated names and domains — the blocker should not even surface this. Trivial true negative (sanity anchor).
Unrelated on every axis. Trivial true negative.
Unrelated names/domains. Trivial true negative.
Apostrophe/punctuation variation ('Chotchkie's' vs 'Chotchkies') on a shared domain. Same.
Pure casing difference on a shared domain. Same.
Punctuation ('n vs n) + suffix variation on a shared domain. Same.
www + suffix on a shared domain; multiword name matches. Same.
Token subset ('Paper Company' dropped) on a shared domain. Same. (Contrasts er-0046, where a Dunder-Mifflin EMPLOYEE entity must NOT fuse with a customer.)
A breakaway company vs the original — related in the world but distinct entities on distinct domains. No shared-domain signal. Must stay apart.

One side's only domain is free-mail (hotmail.com), the other is the real corporate domain. Even with identical names, the free-mail side is not identity evidence, and the domains differ. Must stay apart.

SAME confusable stem as the er-0022 positive but here the DOMAINS DIFFER (vandelay-industries.com vs vandelay-imports.com) — so they are two different companies. Proves the decision rides on domain, not name similarity. Must stay apart.

DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT: parent (P&G) and a consumer brand it owns, BOTH carrying the parent's domain pg.com in CRM. Distinct entities, distinct deal scopes. A domain-alone auto-merge fuses them — exactly the leak min_independent_keys exists to stop. Must stay apart.

DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT: conglomerate vs one of its brands; the brand's CRM record was enriched with the parent's corporate domain. Two entities, one domain. Domain alone must not merge. Must stay apart.
DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT: holding company vs a wholly-owned subsidiary whose record carries the holding domain. Separate legal entities, separate data scopes. Must stay apart.

DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT: two unrelated small businesses whose CRM domain field holds their shared marketing AGENCY's domain (agency-managed email/website). The domain identifies the agency, not either client. Must stay apart.

DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT: two coworking-space members using the space's shared member domain. Shared infrastructure, not shared identity — the co-tenancy failure on a domain that is NOT in any free-mail denylist. Must stay apart.
DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT: franchisor vs an independent franchise operator whose contacts use brand-domain email. The franchisee is its own company with its own contracts and scope. Must stay apart.
DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT: two unrelated university spinouts whose records inherited the founders' .edu domain from contact enrichment. Institutional domains are co-tenant domains. Must stay apart.

DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT: two small businesses on an ISP mail domain (comcast.net) that is deliberately NOT in the free-mail denylist — proves the denylist cannot enumerate every shared-infrastructure domain, so the structural min_independent_keys guard must exist independently. Must stay apart.

DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT: two SIBLING subsidiaries of one holding group (Helios Group), both on the parent's domain. Merging siblings through the parent domain unions two unrelated books of business. Must stay apart.
DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT: two marketplace sellers whose 'website' field holds the marketplace's domain. Platform domain, not company identity. Must stay apart.
DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT: two companies using the same PEO/employer-of-record, whose HR-sourced contacts share the PEO's client mail domain. Shared back office, distinct companies. Must stay apart.

DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT: a distributor whose record carries its MANUFACTURER's domain (rep works from the vendor's portal/email) vs the manufacturer itself. Supply-chain adjacency, not identity. Must stay apart.

DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT: a recently ACQUIRED company whose mailboxes migrated to the acquirer's domain vs the acquirer. Their pre-acquisition data scopes remain distinct; fusing them is a human decision (admin crosswalk), never a domain-alone auto-merge. Must stay apart.

DOMAIN-SHARED-BUT-DISTINCT: two divisions of a conglomerate (Thorne Group) sharing the group domain. Divisions transact independently; a shared group domain must not weld their scopes. Must stay apart.

SHARED-EMAIL-BUT-DISTINCT: one fractional CFO (m.tran@ledgerpartners.co) is the billing contact for TWO unrelated companies. An exact shared customer-contact email between two ACCOUNT records is one shared human, not one company — email alone must not auto-merge accounts. Must stay apart.

SHARED-EMAIL-BUT-DISTINCT: a serial founder's personal gmail is the contact on both of their (distinct) companies. The free-mail DOMAIN is denylisted upstream, but the exact ADDRESS still matches — one person owning two companies does not make them one entity. Must stay apart.
SHARED-EMAIL-BUT-DISTINCT: an agency-of-record account manager is the listed contact on two client accounts. Shared vendor human, distinct customers. Must stay apart.

SHARED-EMAIL-BUT-DISTINCT with a ROLE local part: info@ is a denylisted role account (§4.1 denylist_values) and must never form a key at all — this pair documents the denylist guard working (no key ⇒ no merge signal), independent of min_independent_keys. Must stay apart.

EXTERNAL-ID NEAR-COLLISION: the same bare numeral '88213' in two DIFFERENT id namespaces (a HubSpot company id vs a NetSuite customer id). An external_id key is only a key WITHIN its namespace — cross-namespace value equality is noise. The namespaced scorer must refuse it. Must stay apart.

EXTERNAL-ID NEAR-MISS in the SAME namespace: ACC-00512 vs ACC-0512 — a plausible fat-finger. Exact equality (never normalization/fuzzy) is the external_id contract; the scorer must not 'helpfully' canonicalize digits. Must stay apart.
Sanity anchor: BOTH sides carry all three key kinds and NONE match. Keeps the key-eligible denominators honest (an eligible pair that correctly stays apart). Trivial true negative.

SINGLE-STRONG-KEY TP (external_id only): a sync integration wrote the HubSpot company id onto the Salesforce record before either side was enriched with a domain. The exact namespaced crosswalk is an intentional assertion of identity by the integration — the canonical clean external_id case. Same.
SINGLE-STRONG-KEY TP (external_id only): Gong stores the Salesforce account id it was linked against. Exact crosswalk, no domain on either record. Same.
SINGLE-STRONG-KEY TP (external_id only): both CRMs carry the same ERP (NetSuite) customer id. Names vary (token subset), domains absent — the crosswalk alone links them. Same.
SINGLE-STRONG-KEY TP (external_id only): same ERP account code, abbreviated name variant, no domains. Contrast er-0088: equality is exact ('ACC-00777' == 'ACC-00777'), not fuzzy. Same.

SINGLE-STRONG-KEY TP (verified domain only): exact shared registrable domain, agreeing names, NO email/external_id anywhere. Under min_independent_keys=2 for domain this true dup is FORGONE as an auto-merge (it must route to Tier-2 review) — the measured recall cost of the domain=2 bar. Same.
SINGLE-STRONG-KEY TP (verified domain only): shared .io domain, suffix-only name variance, no second key. Auto-merge forgone under domain=2; surfaces via Tier-2 review instead. Same.
SINGLE-STRONG-KEY TP (verified domain only): shared dev-TLD domain, token-subset names, no second key. Same.
SINGLE-STRONG-KEY TP (verified domain only): casing + suffix variance on one shared domain, no second key. Same.

SINGLE-STRONG-KEY TP (customer-contact email only): a Gong account with NO domain captured, linked to the CRM account solely by the exact contact email. (The email's own domain equals the right side's domain — email and domain are CORRELATED keys here, a caveat the sweep documents.) Same.
SINGLE-STRONG-KEY TP (customer-contact email only): support tracker org with no domain field; the exact reporter email is the only shared key. Same.
SINGLE-STRONG-KEY TP (customer-contact email only): neither record has a domain; the exact named-person contact email alone links them. Same.
SINGLE-STRONG-KEY TP (customer-contact email only): ampersand/'and' name variance, no domains, exact shared contact email. Same.
TWO-KEY TP (domain + email): the pair every min_independent_keys=2 policy still auto-merges — two distinct key kinds agree. (Correlated-key caveat: the email lives on the shared domain.) Same.
TWO-KEY TP (domain + external_id): genuinely independent key kinds agree (a synced crosswalk id plus the verified domain) — auto-merges under every swept policy. Same.
